scenario.prompt_to_agent:
IT and CS Dept users report they cannot reach Server Room or
Internet Lab. router0 and router2 both report RIP routes intact
and can ping each other's interfaces directly. office_pc (on
router1's own LAN) can still ping its gateway 192.168.3.1, but it
too cannot reach the Server Room. What breaks transit through
router1?

injection.action: drop all transit forwarding on router1 (net.ipv4.ip_forward is not writable from the exec context, so use the iptables equivalent: a FORWARD-chain drop)

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router1 packet forwarding (FORWARD chain)
Mechanism: A FORWARD-chain DROP rule makes router1 drop every
  packet it would route BETWEEN interfaces (transit). Transit
  traffic (it_hod -> router0 -> router1 -> router2 -> pc1) is
  dropped at router1, and office_pc -> Server Room is dropped
  too (it is also transit). Only traffic to router1's OWN
  interfaces still works -- office_pc can still ping its gateway
  192.168.3.1 -- which is the tell that router1 is up but not
  forwarding. RIP keeps running because its sockets are local,
  not forwarded. (This is the iptables equivalent of
  net.ipv4.ip_forward=0, used because that sysctl is not writable
  from the exec context.)
Localization: router1
Root cause: a FORWARD-chain DROP rule on router1 stops transit
  forwarding (equivalent to ip_forward disabled)
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP` on router1 (re-enable forwarding)
scoring_axes: must-identify-component: packet forwarding disabled (FORWARD-chain drop / ip_forward)

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: router1’s kernel firewall (netfilter/iptables), specifically the FORWARD chain.

Mechanism: Transit packets that need to cross router1 (e.g., from IT/CS LANs behind router0 to Server Room/Internet Lab behind router2, or even office_pc to Server Room) are evaluated by router1’s FORWARD chain. An unconditional DROP there discards all forwarded traffic. Locally terminated traffic to router1 itself (e.g., office_pc -> 192.168.3.1) hits INPUT and succeeds, and traffic originated by router1 (e.g., router1 pinging 1.0.0.5 or 128.168.0.5) uses OUTPUT and succeeds. Routing tables and RIP adjacencies stay “intact,” so routers can ping each other’s interfaces, masking the issue at the control plane.

Localization: router1, netfilter FORWARD chain; this impacts forwarding between eth0/eth1 (192.168.3.0/24, 192.168.4.0/24) and the WAN links eth2/eth3 (10.10.0.0/8 to router0, 20.20.0.0/8 to router2).

Evidence: On router1, ip_forward=1 and RIP routes are present, and router1 can ping 20.20.0.2, 1.0.0.5, 128.168.0.5. However, iptables shows “-A FORWARD -j DROP” with counters increasing (21 drops). End hosts (it_lab1, cs_lab1, office_pc) time out to remote subnets but can ping 192.168.3.1.

Root cause: A misconfigured blanket iptables rule on router1’s FORWARD chain is dropping all transit traffic.

Corrective fix: Remove or reorder the drop rule (e.g., iptables -D FORWARD -j DROP), or add explicit ACCEPT rules for inter-VLAN/WAN traffic and set FORWARD policy appropriately. Persist the fix via the firewall management service or saved iptables config, ensuring only intended traffic is filtered. RIP needs no changes.

per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly identifies router1 (its netfilter/iptables FORWARD chain) as the faulty device.
